prompt:
Write a narrative account of about 800 words of John Snow's investigation of the 1854 cholera outbreak around Broad Street in London. The reader is a general reader with no medical background.

Do not use dashes, semicolons, colons or parentheses.

text:
In the last days of August 1854, the crowded London district of Soho began to die. The illness was cholera, a disease that brings violent sickness and diarrhoea and can drain a healthy adult of fluid so quickly that death arrives within a day. Families in the streets around Broad Street, a busy road of workshops, lodging houses and small shops, fell ill by the dozen. Within about ten days, hundreds were dead. Many survivors fled the neighbourhood, leaving shuttered houses behind them.

Most doctors of the day agreed on what caused such outbreaks. They blamed miasma, a poisonous foul smelling air that was thought to rise from rotting waste and filthy ground. London in the 1850s certainly stank. The river carried sewage, cesspools overflowed under floorboards, and the summer heat made it all worse. The theory seemed sensible to anyone who walked through the slums with a handkerchief over their nose.

John Snow did not believe it. Snow was a physician in his early forties, the son of a Yorkshire labourer, who had risen through hard work and a sharp mind. He was already famous in medical circles for his careful work on anaesthesia, and he had given chloroform to Queen Victoria during childbirth. He was a quiet man who did not drink alcohol and ate plainly. He also had a habit that would define his career, which was to count things and trust the numbers.

Years before, during an earlier cholera epidemic in 1848 and 1849, Snow had formed a different idea. Cholera, he reasoned, attacked the gut first. Victims suffered in their stomachs and bowels, not in their lungs, which is where a poisonous air would do its harm. So the cause must be something swallowed, and it must be passed from one person to the next through contaminated water or food. He had published his thoughts in a short pamphlet, and most colleagues had politely ignored it.

When the Soho outbreak began, Snow lived only a short walk away, and he saw his chance to test his idea. He started by doing something that sounds obvious now but was unusual then. He went door to door. He asked families who had died, where they had lived, and what they had drunk. He obtained the official list of deaths and marked each address on a street map with a small black bar. As the bars piled up, a pattern appeared. They clustered thickly around one spot, the public water pump on Broad Street, where residents drew their drinking water by hand.

The map was striking, but Snow knew that a cluster alone proved little. The strongest evidence came from the exceptions. Nearby stood a workhouse housing more than five hundred poor people. Almost none of them died. Snow discovered that the workhouse had its own private well and never used the Broad Street pump. A brewery on the same street also lost no workers, and its men were given beer to drink and had their own supply of water besides. Then there were the strange cases far away. A widow who lived in Hampstead, miles from Soho, died of cholera after her son sent her bottles of water from the Broad Street pump, because she liked its taste. A lady in Pimlico who did the same also died. Nobody else in their neighbourhoods fell ill.

On the evening of 7 September, Snow took his findings to the local board of guardians, the men responsible for the parish. He urged them to act. The next day they removed the handle from the pump, so that no one could draw water from it. The outbreak was already fading by then, partly because so many people had fled, and sceptics would later say the handle had made no difference. Snow himself was careful on this point. He never claimed the handle alone ended the epidemic.

Help came from an unexpected direction. A local clergyman named Henry Whitehead, who knew his parishioners well, began as a doubter of Snow's theory. He set out to prove it wrong, and instead ended up strengthening it. Whitehead tracked down the likely first case, a baby girl who had fallen ill at a house on Broad Street just before the outbreak. Her mother had washed the child's soiled cloths and thrown the dirty water into a cesspool that, as workmen later found, leaked close to the well. The source of the poison had been found.

The authorities were not convinced. An official inquiry concluded that the water was not to blame, and Snow died in 1858, aged only forty five, still regarded by many as an eccentric. Only later did scientists identify the tiny living organism that causes cholera and confirm that it spreads through dirty water. The slow shift in public health that followed, with clean water supplies and proper sewers, owed a great deal to him. Snow had shown that a careful map, patient questions and honest counting could do what theory and fear had never managed.
